commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop

commands.name: docs
commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: computer-use
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: chrome-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: built-in-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: anthropic-skills:deep-research
commands.description: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: setup-writing-style

The profile is saved as the my-writing-style skill. Use when the user asks to set up, learn, or capture their writing voice, or complains that drafts sound generic or unlike them and no my-writing-style profile exists. Only for drafting text the user will send as themselves, not for Claude's own replies. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: skill-creator
commands.description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pdf
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

1	<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 -->
2	<!-- Cut byte for byte from spike/mermaid/PRE-REGISTRATION.md by harness/ms/blind.py:
3	     its sections 4 and 5, Appendices A and C, and Appendix D's extractor contract
4	     (its heading and its Extractor paragraph), in that order. -->
5	## 4. The model
6	
7	### 4.1 Classes
8	
9	| class | content |
10	|---|---|
11	| **identity** | one namespace of keys, each with a kind: `node` (a node id), `subgraph` (an explicit subgraph id, or `title:` plus the title for a subgraph Mermaid numbers itself) or `edge` (an explicit edge id, `e1@-->`, that R marks `isUserDefinedId`) |
12	| **relation** | edges, as a multiset of `(from key, to key, kind, label)`. An edge with a user-defined id is keyed by that id instead. An edge end that names a subgraph is a reference to that subgraph (Appendix A) |
13	| **membership** | for each node and subgraph, the subgraph that holds it, or none |
14	| **text** | each node's label; each subgraph's title; each edge label; `click` targets |
15	| **shape** | each node's shape, or `none` for a node with no shape statement |
16	| **style** | `classDef`, `class`, `:::`, `style`, `linkStyle`; direction statements |
17	| **order** | statement order (layout only) |
18	
19	Appendix A maps each class from R's output.
20	
21	### 4.2 Units
22	
23	The oracle decides each unit separately:
24	
25	- a key's existence, and its kind;
26	- a scalar value: `(key, property)`;
27	- an edge key's count;
28	- a membership: `(key)` mapped to its holder;
29	- a class assignment: `(key, class)`.
30	
31	A unit is **keyed by** `k` if it is `k`'s existence, kind, scalar, membership
32	or class. A unit **refers to** `k` if it is keyed by `k` or holds `k` as a
33	value: an edge end, a class or style target, or a click target.
34	
35	**A membership's holder is not a reference.** Membership is block containment:
36	a member is a line inside the holder's `subgraph … end` block, and git carries
37	it with the block. Renaming, retitling or unwrapping the block moves the
38	member with it. So a membership unit is **undecided**, and not a model
39	conflict, whenever its decided holder, or any of its holder values in `B`,
40	`O` or `T`, is a key that is decided absent. An undecided membership yields no
41	I1, no G3 and no MC, and it does not make a case exposed (§5.5). This covers a
42	member moved from one box to another on one leg while the other leg renames or
43	retitles both boxes: git merges it correctly, and no holder value the legs
44	wrote survives as a key. `census/synth-results.out` shows this on synthetic cases (§11.2, V3).
45	
46	### 4.3 Three parsers
47	
48	- **H**, the harness parser. Pure-stdlib Python. It accepts the subset in
49	  Appendix A and nothing else.
50	- **R**, the renderer: Mermaid 12.1.0, run as §4.4 pins. A text **parses** if
51	  R's parse succeeds. R also yields a model, mapped as Appendix A says.
52	- **X**, the second extractor, written blind (§10).
53	
54	**A blob is in the subset** only if H parses it and H's model equals R's model.
55	Where Mermaid's behaviour decides a value, H must agree with R or the blob is
56	out of the subset. Appendix A lists each such behaviour as observed in
57	`census/v0-probes.out`. **A value H computes that Appendix A does not map from
58	R is never compared for tier A.**
59	
60	### 4.4 R, pinned
61	
62	- Node v24.20.0 (Mermaid 12.1.0 declares `node >=22.12.0`).
63	- `mermaid@12.1.0` and `jsdom@26.1.0`, pinned by a committed
64	  `package-lock.json` with integrity hashes, installed with `--ignore-scripts`.
65	  The synthetic probes ran on an install that resolved `dompurify@3.4.16`.
66	- **The wrapper** creates a jsdom window and sets `globalThis.window` and
67	  `globalThis.document` **before** it imports Mermaid. Without them DOMPurify
68	  defines no `sanitize`, and any chart with a label throws a `TypeError`
69	  (`census/v0-probes.out`, probe2 with `NO_JSDOM=1`).
70	- `mermaid.initialize({startOnLoad: false, securityLevel: "strict",
71	  maxEdges: 100000, flowchart: {htmlLabels: false}})`. With Mermaid's default,
72	  a chart of 500 or more edges throws "Edge limit exceeded" (probe2 with
73	  `DEFAULT_EDGES=1`). A chart over 100,000 edges is out of the subset and
74	  counted.
75	- **What "does not parse" means.** The wrapper calls `mermaid.parse(text)`
76	  and never passes `suppressErrors`, which turns every failure, a broken
77	  toolchain included, into `false` (probe5).
78	  - A thrown error that carries jison's `hash` property: the text does not
79	    parse.
80	  - **Any other thrown error:** the wrapper re-parses the fixed canary
81	    `flowchart TD` / `A[Alpha] --> B`. If the canary parses, the text does not
82	    parse, and the error class and first message line are recorded. If the
83	    canary fails, the toolchain is broken and the run aborts with a non-zero
84	    exit.
85	  - Texts whose errors carry no `hash` include an out-of-range `linkStyle`
86	    (`TypeError`), an unknown `@{ shape: … }` (`Error`, "No such shape"), a
87	    mixed-case header (`UnknownDiagramError`) and the edge limit (`Error`,
88	    "Edge limit exceeded"). Without jsdom, a labelled chart throws a
89	    `TypeError` and so does the canary, so the run aborts
90	    (`census/v4-error-texts.out`).
91	  - "Does not parse" makes a merged file E, and an input out of the subset.
92	- The model is read with `mermaid.mermaidAPI.getDiagramFromText(text)` and
93	  its flowchart database.
94	- No network after install.
95	
96	
97	## 5. The oracle
98	
99	### 5.1 Decided values
100	
101	Three model states: base `B`, legs `O` and `T`. For each unit:
102	
103	- if `O` and `T` agree, that value is **decided**;
104	- if only one leg differs from `B`, that leg's value is decided;
105	- otherwise it is a **model conflict**.
106	
107	Keys are the identity. A renamed id is a removed key and an added key. The
108	oracle does not guess renames.
109	
110	### 5.2 Refusal cases
111	
112	Some decided models cannot be rendered correctly by any merge. The only
113	correct outcome is then E. These are:
114	
115	- **dangling**: a decided-present unit refers to a key that is decided
116	  absent (a membership's holder is not a reference, §4.2);
117	- **collision**: a key is absent in `B`, both legs add it, and some unit keyed
118	  by it differs between `O` and `T`, its kind included;
119	- **delete/modify**: one leg removes a key, and the other changes a unit keyed
120	  by it.
121	
122	### 5.3 Categories
123	
124	**E (loud).** A path is E if its merged file holds a conflict marker, or `git
125	ls-files -u -- <path>` is not empty, or R does not parse the merged diagram
126	(§4.4). For stratum D, a conflict anywhere in the file makes it E. A conflict
127	on another path in the same merge does not.
128	
129	Every other category needs a path that is not E and four states in the
130	subset. A merged state outside the subset is **OUT-OF-SUBSET**: counted and
131	listed, never decided.
132	
133	**DUP-TITLE** is its own listed outcome. When both legs add a subgraph without
134	an explicit id under the same title, git keeps both blocks, and the merged
135	state has two such subgraphs with one title. Neither leg's inputs are out of
136	the subset, but the merged state is, because §4.1 keys them by title. It is
137	counted and listed under its own name, never decided, and it counts toward
138	`k` when the case is exposed (§9.1).
139	
140	**A record's objects** are the keys it concerns: for I1, the removed key and
141	every key of each unit that refers to it; for I2, I3 and I4, the key; for G1,
142	the node; for G2, the edge's two ends and its edge id if any; for G3, the
143	member and both holders, decided and merged; for G4, the key of the text unit,
144	or the edge's two ends; for G0, the path.
145	
146	**Identity group.**
147	
148	- **I1 Dangling resolved.** A dangling refusal case merged clean. This is
149	  hole #2.
150	- **I2 Collision merged.** A collision merged clean. This is hole #3.
151	- **I3 Delete/modify merged.** A delete/modify merged clean.
152	- **I4 Kind clash.** A key that no input gives two kinds, or a kind other than
153	  its decided kind, has two kinds or a different kind in the merged model. A
154	  clash already present in an input is not a record. R drops a node statement
155	  whose id was used earlier as an edge id (probe), so this is an identity
156	  fault, not a G1. An edge end that names a subgraph is a reference, not a
157	  clash (Appendix A).
158	
159	**Structure group.**
160	
161	- **G0 Diagram.** The merged file no longer holds exactly one Mermaid fence, or
162	  its diagram is no longer a flowchart.
163	- **G1 Node.** A decided-present node is absent, or a decided-absent node is
164	  present, outside I1–I4.
165	- **G2 Edge.** An edge key's merged count differs from the decided count. Lost
166	  and extra are reported apart.
167	- **G3 Membership.** A membership differs from the decided holder.
168	- **G4 Label.** A text unit differs from the decided value.
169	
170	**Other.**
171	
172	- **MC.** A model conflict outside §5.2 merged clean. It is eligible only if
173	  the merged value is neither leg's value. It then takes the group of its
174	  class: relation G2, membership G3, text G4, shape C, style D.
175	- **C, shape.** A shape unit differs from the decided value.
176	- **D, style.** A style unit differs. A `linkStyle` that lands on a different
177	  edge, because it addresses edges by position, is **S-LINKSTYLE**, tier D.
178	- **S-ORDER.** Statement order differs. Layout only. Reported, never eligible.
179	
180	An edge written to a positional id, such as `X --> subGraph0`, is rare, and it
181	retargets when a leg inserts an untitled subgraph earlier. The oracle keys the
182	edge end by the subgraph it names in each state, so this lands in **G2**, as a
183	lost edge and an extra edge (`census/synth-results.out`, `posRef`).
184	
185	### 5.4 Tiers, computed
186	
187	| tier | categories | qualifies |
188	|---|---|---|
189	| **A** | I1–I4 (identity group); G1–G4 and eligible MC of relation, membership or text (structure group) | yes, for its group's verdict |
190	| **B** | any A record one of whose objects newly fails a lint (row 1); every G0 record | no: a lint over existing Mermaid catches it |
191	| **C** | shape | no: a near miss |
192	| **D** | style, S-LINKSTYLE | no |
193	| **E** | E | no: git refused |
194	| — | S-ORDER, ineligible MC, OUT-OF-SUBSET | reported only |
195	
196	A lint failure is **new** if the same `(lint, object)` is absent from all
197	three inputs. Only new failures matter. A chart written in bare `A --> B`
198	style already fails L1 on every node, so L1 never demotes a record there.
199	
200	### 5.5 Exposure
201	
202	A case is **exposed** if its inputs meet a refusal case's precondition, read
203	from `B`, `O` and `T` only:
204	
205	- one leg removes a key that a unit added or changed by the other leg refers
206	  to; or
207	- both legs add the same key with some differing unit keyed by it.
208	
209	Exposure is computed before the merge result is read. An exposed case that
210	comes out E or B is git or a lint working.
211	
212	
213	## Appendix A — the subset, and R's model
214	
215	**In the subset:**
216	
217	- a header `flowchart`, `flowchart-elk` or `graph`, with an optional direction
218	  (`TB`, `TD`, `BT`, `LR`, `RL`);
219	- leading front matter and `%%{init: …}%%` directives, read as configuration
220	  and ignored by the model;
221	- `%%` comments;
222	- node statements with the classic shapes: `[ ]`, `( )`, `([ ])`, `[[ ]]`,
223	  `[( )]`, `(( ))`, `> ]`, `{ }`, `{{ }}`, `[/ /]`, `[\ \]`, `[/ \]`,
224	  `[\ /]`, `((( )))`; quoted labels; and the `@{ shape: …, label: … }` form;
225	- edges `-->`, `---`, `-.->`, `-.-`, `==>`, `===`, `~~~`, `--o`, `--x`,
226	  `<-->`, `o--o`, `x--x`, with extra-length variants; labels as `-->|text|`
227	  and `-- text -->`; chains `A --> B --> C`; `&` groups; edge ids `e1@-->`;
228	- `subgraph id [title]`, `subgraph id`, and `subgraph Some Title` or
229	  `subgraph "Some title"` (no explicit id) … `end`, nested, with `direction`
230	  inside;
231	- `classDef`, `class`, `:::`, `style`, `linkStyle`, `click`.
232	
233	**Out of the subset, each refused and counted:** Markdown-string labels
234	(`` "`…`" ``), icon and image node forms, `@{ … }` keys other than `shape`
235	and `label`, two subgraphs without an explicit id that share a title, an
236	explicit subgraph id of the form `subGraphN` (R merges it with its own
237	numbering, V0), an edge end that names a user-defined edge id (V0), and any
238	statement H does not parse. A text that does not parse under §4.4's rule is
239	not an input in the subset.
240	
241	**A node statement** is an occurrence of an id followed by a shape bracket, or
242	by `@{ … }`, whether alone or inside an edge chain. A bare id is not a node
243	statement. L1 reads this definition.
244	
245	**R's model, class by class.** Each line cites the probe in
246	`census/v0-probes.out` that shows the behaviour; V0 repeats each.
247	
248	- **identity.**
249	  - Node keys are the vertex map's keys, except a vertex whose id equals a
250	    subgraph's id and that has no node statement anywhere in the text: that is
251	    an edge end referring to the subgraph (probe `edgeToSub`).
252	  - A subgraph's key is its `id` if the text gave one, and `title:` plus its
253	    title if R assigned `subGraphN` because the header had no explicit id

## 4. The model

### 4.1 Classes

| class | content |
|---|---|
| **identity** | one namespace of keys, each with a kind: `node` (a node id), `subgraph` (an explicit subgraph id, or `title:` plus the title for a subgraph Mermaid numbers itself) or `edge` (an explicit edge id, `e1@-->`, that R marks `isUserDefinedId`) |
| **relation** | edges, as a multiset of `(from key, to key, kind, label)`. An edge with a user-defined id is keyed by that id instead. An edge end that names a subgraph is a reference to that subgraph (Appendix A) |
| **membership** | for each node and subgraph, the subgraph that holds it, or none |
| **text** | each node's label; each subgraph's title; each edge label; `click` targets |
| **shape** | each node's shape, or `none` for a node with no shape statement |
| **style** | `classDef`, `class`, `:::`, `style`, `linkStyle`; direction statements |
| **order** | statement order (layout only) |

Appendix A maps each class from R's output.

### 4.2 Units

The oracle decides each unit separately:

- a key's existence, and its kind;
- a scalar value: `(key, property)`;
- an edge key's count;
- a membership: `(key)` mapped to its holder;
- a class assignment: `(key, class)`.

A unit is **keyed by** `k` if it is `k`'s existence, kind, scalar, membership
or class. A unit **refers to** `k` if it is keyed by `k` or holds `k` as a
value: an edge end, a class or style target, or a click target.

**A membership's holder is not a reference.** Membership is block containment:
a member is a line inside the holder's `subgraph … end` block, and git carries
it with the block. Renaming, retitling or unwrapping the block moves the
member with it. So a membership unit is **undecided**, and not a model
conflict, whenever its decided holder, or any of its holder values in `B`,
`O` or `T`, is a key that is decided absent. An undecided membership yields no
I1, no G3 and no MC, and it does not make a case exposed (§5.5). This covers a
member moved from one box to another on one leg while the other leg renames or
retitles both boxes: git merges it correctly, and no holder value the legs
wrote survives as a key. `census/synth-results.out` shows this on synthetic cases (§11.2, V3).

### 4.3 Three parsers

- **H**, the harness parser. Pure-stdlib Python. It accepts the subset in
  Appendix A and nothing else.
- **R**, the renderer: Mermaid 12.1.0, run as §4.4 pins. A text **parses** if
  R's parse succeeds. R also yields a model, mapped as Appendix A says.
- **X**, the second extractor, written blind (§10).

**A blob is in the subset** only if H parses it and H's model equals R's model.
Where Mermaid's behaviour decides a value, H must agree with R or the blob is
out of the subset. Appendix A lists each such behaviour as observed in
`census/v0-probes.out`. **A value H computes that Appendix A does not map from
R is never compared for tier A.**

### 4.4 R, pinned

- Node v24.20.0 (Mermaid 12.1.0 declares `node >=22.12.0`).
- `mermaid@12.1.0` and `jsdom@26.1.0`, pinned by a committed
  `package-lock.json` with integrity hashes, installed with `--ignore-scripts`.
  The synthetic probes ran on an install that resolved `dompurify@3.4.16`.
- **The wrapper** creates a jsdom window and sets `globalThis.window` and
  `globalThis.document` **before** it imports Mermaid. Without them DOMPurify
  defines no `sanitize`, and any chart with a label throws a `TypeError`
  (`census/v0-probes.out`, probe2 with `NO_JSDOM=1`).
- `mermaid.initialize({startOnLoad: false, securityLevel: "strict",
  maxEdges: 100000, flowchart: {htmlLabels: false}})`. With Mermaid's default,
  a chart of 500 or more edges throws "Edge limit exceeded" (probe2 with
  `DEFAULT_EDGES=1`). A chart over 100,000 edges is out of the subset and
  counted.
- **What "does not parse" means.** The wrapper calls `mermaid.parse(text)`
  and never passes `suppressErrors`, which turns every failure, a broken
  toolchain included, into `false` (probe5).
  - A thrown error that carries jison's `hash` property: the text does not
    parse.
  - **Any other thrown error:** the wrapper re-parses the fixed canary
    `flowchart TD` / `A[Alpha] --> B`. If the canary parses, the text does not
    parse, and the error class and first message line are recorded. If the
    canary fails, the toolchain is broken and the run aborts with a non-zero
    exit.
  - Texts whose errors carry no `hash` include an out-of-range `linkStyle`
    (`TypeError`), an unknown `@{ shape: … }` (`Error`, "No such shape"), a
    mixed-case header (`UnknownDiagramError`) and the edge limit (`Error`,
    "Edge limit exceeded"). Without jsdom, a labelled chart throws a
    `TypeError` and so does the canary, so the run aborts
    (`census/v4-error-texts.out`).
  - "Does not parse" makes a merged file E, and an input out of the subset.
- The model is read with `mermaid.mermaidAPI.getDiagramFromText(text)` and
  its flowchart database.
- No network after install.


## 5. The oracle

### 5.1 Decided values

Three model states: base `B`, legs `O` and `T`. For each unit:

- if `O` and `T` agree, that value is **decided**;
- if only one leg differs from `B`, that leg's value is decided;
- otherwise it is a **model conflict**.

Keys are the identity. A renamed id is a removed key and an added key. The
oracle does not guess renames.

### 5.2 Refusal cases

Some decided models cannot be rendered correctly by any merge. The only
correct outcome is then E. These are:

- **dangling**: a decided-present unit refers to a key that is decided
  absent (a membership's holder is not a reference, §4.2);
- **collision**: a key is absent in `B`, both legs add it, and some unit keyed
  by it differs between `O` and `T`, its kind included;
- **delete/modify**: one leg removes a key, and the other changes a unit keyed
  by it.

### 5.3 Categories

**E (loud).** A path is E if its merged file holds a conflict marker, or `git
ls-files -u -- <path>` is not empty, or R does not parse the merged diagram
(§4.4). For stratum D, a conflict anywhere in the file makes it E. A conflict
on another path in the same merge does not.

Every other category needs a path that is not E and four states in the
subset. A merged state outside the subset is **OUT-OF-SUBSET**: counted and
listed, never decided.

**DUP-TITLE** is its own listed outcome. When both legs add a subgraph without
an explicit id under the same title, git keeps both blocks, and the merged
state has two such subgraphs with one title. Neither leg's inputs are out of
the subset, but the merged state is, because §4.1 keys them by title. It is
counted and listed under its own name, never decided, and it counts toward
`k` when the case is exposed (§9.1).

**A record's objects** are the keys it concerns: for I1, the removed key and
every key of each unit that refers to it; for I2, I3 and I4, the key; for G1,
the node; for G2, the edge's two ends and its edge id if any; for G3, the
member and both holders, decided and merged; for G4, the key of the text unit,
or the edge's two ends; for G0, the path.

**Identity group.**

- **I1 Dangling resolved.** A dangling refusal case merged clean. This is
  hole #2.
- **I2 Collision merged.** A collision merged clean. This is hole #3.
- **I3 Delete/modify merged.** A delete/modify merged clean.
- **I4 Kind clash.** A key that no input gives two kinds, or a kind other than
  its decided kind, has two kinds or a different kind in the merged model. A
  clash already present in an input is not a record. R drops a node statement
  whose id was used earlier as an edge id (probe), so this is an identity
  fault, not a G1. An edge end that names a subgraph is a reference, not a
  clash (Appendix A).

**Structure group.**

- **G0 Diagram.** The merged file no longer holds exactly one Mermaid fence, or
  its diagram is no longer a flowchart.
- **G1 Node.** A decided-present node is absent, or a decided-absent node is
  present, outside I1–I4.
- **G2 Edge.** An edge key's merged count differs from the decided count. Lost
  and extra are reported apart.
- **G3 Membership.** A membership differs from the decided holder.
- **G4 Label.** A text unit differs from the decided value.

**Other.**

- **MC.** A model conflict outside §5.2 merged clean. It is eligible only if
  the merged value is neither leg's value. It then takes the group of its
  class: relation G2, membership G3, text G4, shape C, style D.
- **C, shape.** A shape unit differs from the decided value.
- **D, style.** A style unit differs. A `linkStyle` that lands on a different
  edge, because it addresses edges by position, is **S-LINKSTYLE**, tier D.
- **S-ORDER.** Statement order differs. Layout only. Reported, never eligible.

An edge written to a positional id, such as `X --> subGraph0`, is rare, and it
retargets when a leg inserts an untitled subgraph earlier. The oracle keys the
edge end by the subgraph it names in each state, so this lands in **G2**, as a
lost edge and an extra edge (`census/synth-results.out`, `posRef`).

### 5.4 Tiers, computed

| tier | categories | qualifies |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | I1–I4 (identity group); G1–G4 and eligible MC of relation, membership or text (structure group) | yes, for its group's verdict |
| **B** | any A record one of whose objects newly fails a lint (row 1); every G0 record | no: a lint over existing Mermaid catches it |
| **C** | shape | no: a near miss |
| **D** | style, S-LINKSTYLE | no |
| **E** | E | no: git refused |
| — | S-ORDER, ineligible MC, OUT-OF-SUBSET | reported only |

A lint failure is **new** if the same `(lint, object)` is absent from all
three inputs. Only new failures matter. A chart written in bare `A --> B`
style already fails L1 on every node, so L1 never demotes a record there.

### 5.5 Exposure

A case is **exposed** if its inputs meet a refusal case's precondition, read
from `B`, `O` and `T` only:

- one leg removes a key that a unit added or changed by the other leg refers
  to; or
- both legs add the same key with some differing unit keyed by it.

Exposure is computed before the merge result is read. An exposed case that
comes out E or B is git or a lint working.


## Appendix A — the subset, and R's model

**In the subset:**

- a header `flowchart`, `flowchart-elk` or `graph`, with an optional direction
  (`TB`, `TD`, `BT`, `LR`, `RL`);
- leading front matter and `%%{init: …}%%` directives, read as configuration
  and ignored by the model;
- `%%` comments;
- node statements with the classic shapes: `[ ]`, `( )`, `([ ])`, `[[ ]]`,
  `[( )]`, `(( ))`, `> ]`, `{ }`, `{{ }}`, `[/ /]`, `[\ \]`, `[/ \]`,
  `[\ /]`, `((( )))`; quoted labels; and the `@{ shape: …, label: … }` form;
- edges `-->`, `---`, `-.->`, `-.-`, `==>`, `===`, `~~~`, `--o`, `--x`,
  `<-->`, `o--o`, `x--x`, with extra-length variants; labels as `-->|text|`
  and `-- text -->`; chains `A --> B --> C`; `&` groups; edge ids `e1@-->`;
- `subgraph id [title]`, `subgraph id`, and `subgraph Some Title` or
  `subgraph "Some title"` (no explicit id) … `end`, nested, with `direction`
  inside;
- `classDef`, `class`, `:::`, `style`, `linkStyle`, `click`.

**Out of the subset, each refused and counted:** Markdown-string labels
(`` "`…`" ``), icon and image node forms, `@{ … }` keys other than `shape`
and `label`, two subgraphs without an explicit id that share a title, an
explicit subgraph id of the form `subGraphN` (R merges it with its own
numbering, V0), an edge end that names a user-defined edge id (V0), and any
statement H does not parse. A text that does not parse under §4.4's rule is
not an input in the subset.

**A node statement** is an occurrence of an id followed by a shape bracket, or
by `@{ … }`, whether alone or inside an edge chain. A bare id is not a node
statement. L1 reads this definition.

**R's model, class by class.** Each line cites the probe in
`census/v0-probes.out` that shows the behaviour; V0 repeats each.

- **identity.**
  - Node keys are the vertex map's keys, except a vertex whose id equals a
    subgraph's id and that has no node statement anywhere in the text: that is
    an edge end referring to the subgraph (probe `edgeToSub`).
  - A subgraph's key is its `id` if the text gave one, and `title:` plus its
    title if R assigned `subGraphN` because the header had no explicit id
    (probe3, probe4). H decides which from the header form, and must agree
    with R's `id`.
  - An edge key is the edge's `id` when R reports `isUserDefinedId: true`
    (probe2 `edgeIdUser`). Automatic ids are never keys. A second edge with a
    repeated user-defined id gets an automatic id and `isUserDefinedId: false`
    (probe `dupEdgeId`).
  - A node statement for an id already used as an edge id is dropped by R; a
    node declared first coexists with a later edge id of the same name (probes
    `edgeIdThenNode`, `nodeEqEdgeId`).
  - A node id equal to a subgraph id, with a node statement, gives both a node
    and a subgraph (probes `subEqNode`, `subEqNode2`).
- **relation.** Each edge's `start`, `end`, normalized kind, and `text`.
- **membership.** A node's holder is the first subgraph, in R's subgraph list
  order, whose `nodes` list holds it. The list is in closing order, so a node
  mentioned in two subgraphs belongs to the first to close, and an inner
  subgraph closes before its outer one (probes `twoSub`, `twoSubRev`,
  `twoSubNested`).
- **text.** A vertex's `text`, where a node declared twice keeps its last label
  (probe `twice`); a subgraph's `title`; an edge's `text`, compared exactly as
  R reports it, since R does not decode entities in it (probe `labelEdge`); a
  vertex's `link` and `linkTarget` for `click`, as R normalizes them (probe2
  `click`).
- **shape.** A vertex's `type`, where a node declared twice keeps its last
  shape (probe `twiceShape`). A node with no shape statement has no `type`;
  the model records `none` (probe `bare`).
- **style.** A vertex's `classes`, without the class `clickable` that R adds
  for `click` (probe2 `click`), and its `styles`; the class definitions; each
  edge's `style` from `linkStyle`.
- **order.** The order of R's vertex map and edge list.

**Normalization.** Arrow kinds map to `(line, head)`, where line is `solid`,
`dotted`, `thick` or `invisible`, and head is `none`, `arrow`, `circle` or
`cross`, at each end. Extra length is dropped. Node labels and subgraph titles
are compared after trimming outer whitespace. Nothing else is normalized.


## Appendix C — lints for tier B (row 1)

Each runs on the merged file alone. Only a new failure counts (§5.4).

- **L1. Implicit node.** A node id with no node statement (Appendix A).
- **L2. Redeclared node.** A node id given two different labels or shapes.
- **L3. Multi-held node.** A node mentioned inside two different subgraph
  blocks.
- **L4. Id clash.** An id used as two kinds.
- **L5. Duplicate edge.** Two edge statements with the same key.
- **L6. Fence.** For stratum D, the file does not hold exactly one Mermaid
  fence whose diagram is a flowchart.


## Appendix D — contracts for the blind roles

**Extractor.** `python3 -I extract2.py <stratum> <base> <o> <t> <merged>`

426	## Expanded Node Shapes in Mermaid Flowcharts (v11.3.0+)
427	
428	Mermaid introduces 30 new shapes to enhance the flexibility and precision of flowchart creation. These new shapes provide more options to represent processes, decisions, events, data storage visually, and other elements within your flowcharts, improving clarity and semantic meaning.
429	
430	New Syntax for Shape Definition
431	
432	Mermaid now supports a general syntax for defining shape types to accommodate the growing number of shapes. This syntax allows you to assign specific shapes to nodes using a clear and flexible format:
433	
434	```
435	A@{ shape: rect }
436	```
437	
438	This syntax creates a node A as a rectangle. It renders in the same way as `A["A"]`, or `A`.

1074	## Special shapes in Mermaid Flowcharts (v11.3.0+)
1075	
1076	Mermaid also introduces 2 special shapes to enhance your flowcharts: **icon** and **image**. These shapes allow you to include icons and images directly within your flowcharts, providing more visual context and clarity.
1077	
1078	### Icon Shape
1079	
1080	You can use the `icon` shape to include an icon in your flowchart. To use icons, you need to register the icon pack first. Follow the instructions to [add custom icons](../config/icons.md). The syntax for defining an icon shape is as follows:
1081	
1082	```mermaid-example
1083	flowchart TD
1084	    A@{ icon: "fa:user", form: "square", label: "User Icon", pos: "t", h: 60 }
1085	```
1086	
1087	```mermaid
1088	flowchart TD
1089	    A@{ icon: "fa:user", form: "square", label: "User Icon", pos: "t", h: 60 }
1090	```
1091	
1092	#### Parameters
1093	
1094	- **icon**: The name of the icon from the registered icon pack.
1095	- **form**: Specifies the background shape of the icon. If not defined there will be no background to icon. Options include:
1096	  - `square`
1097	  - `circle`
1098	  - `rounded`
1099	- **label**: The text label associated with the icon. This can be any string. If not defined, no label will be displayed.
1100	- **pos**: The position of the label. If not defined label will default to bottom of icon. Possible values are:
1101	  - `t`
1102	  - `b`
1103	- **h**: The height of the icon. If not defined this will default to 48 which is minimum.
1104	
1105	### Image Shape
1106	
1107	You can use the `image` shape to include an image in your flowchart. The syntax for defining an image shape is as follows:
1108	
1109	```
1110	flowchart TD
1111	    A@{ img: "https://example.com/image.png", label: "Image Label", pos: "t", w: 60, h: 60, constraint: "off" }
1112	```
1113	
1114	#### Parameters
1115	
1116	- **img**: The URL of the image to be displayed.
1117	- **label**: The text label associated with the image. This can be any string. If not defined, no label will be displayed.
1118	- **pos**: The position of the label. If not defined, the label will default to the bottom of the image. Possible values are:
1119	  - `t`
1120	  - `b`
1121	- **w**: The width of the image. If not defined, this will default to the natural width of the image.
1122	- **h**: The height of the image. If not defined, this will default to the natural height of the image.
1123	- **constraint**: Determines if the image should constrain the node size. This setting also ensures the image maintains its original aspect ratio, adjusting the width (`w`) accordingly to the height (`h`). If not defined, this will default to `off` Possible values are:
1124	  - `on`
1125	  - `off`
1126	
1127	If you want to resize an image, but keep the same aspect ratio, set `h`, and set `constraint: on` to constrain the aspect ratio. E.g.
1128	
1129	```mermaid-example
1130	flowchart TD
1131	  %% My image with a constrained aspect ratio
1132	  A@{ img: "https://mermaid.js.org/favicon.svg", label: "My example image label", pos: "t", h: 60, constraint: "on" }
1133	```
1134	
1135	```mermaid

1137	  %% My image with a constrained aspect ratio
1138	  A@{ img: "https://mermaid.js.org/favicon.svg", label: "My example image label", pos: "t", h: 60, constraint: "on" }
1139	```

1338	### Attaching an ID to Edges
1339	
1340	Mermaid now supports assigning IDs to edges, similar to how IDs and metadata can be attached to nodes. This feature lays the groundwork for more advanced styling, classes, and animation capabilities on edges.
1341	
1342	**Syntax:**
1343	
1344	To give an edge an ID, prepend the edge syntax with the ID followed by an `@` character. For example:
1345	
1346	```mermaid-example
1347	flowchart LR
1348	  A e1@--> B
1349	```
1350	
1351	```mermaid
1352	flowchart LR
1353	  A e1@--> B
1354	```
1355	
1356	In this example, `e1` is the ID of the edge connecting `A` to `B`. You can then use this ID in later definitions or style statements, just like with nodes.
1357	
1358	### Turning an Animation On
1359	
1360	Once you have assigned an ID to an edge, you can turn on animations for that edge by defining the edge’s properties:
1361	
1362	```mermaid-example
1363	flowchart LR
1364	  A e1@==> B
1365	  e1@{ animate: true }
1366	```
1367	
1368	```mermaid
1369	flowchart LR
1370	  A e1@==> B
1371	  e1@{ animate: true }
1372	```
1373	
1374	This tells Mermaid that the edge `e1` should be animated.
1375	
1376	### Selecting Type of Animation
1377	
1378	In the initial version, two animation speeds are supported: `fast` and `slow`. Selecting a specific animation type is a shorthand for enabling animation and setting the animation speed in one go.
1379	
1380	**Examples:**
1381	
1382	```mermaid-example
1383	flowchart LR
1384	  A e1@--> B
1385	  e1@{ animation: fast }
1386	```
1387	
1388	```mermaid
1389	flowchart LR
1390	  A e1@--> B
1391	  e1@{ animation: fast }
1392	```
1393	
1394	This is equivalent to `{ animate: true, animation: fast }`.
1395	
1396	### Using classDef Statements for Animations
1397	
1398	You can also animate edges by assigning a class to them and then defining animation properties in a `classDef` statement. For example:
1399	
1400	```mermaid-example
1401	flowchart LR
1402	  A e1@--> B
1403	  classDef animate stroke-dasharray: 9,5,stroke-dashoffset: 900,animation: dash 25s linear infinite;
1404	  class e1 animate
1405	```
1406	
1407	```mermaid
1408	flowchart LR
1409	  A e1@--> B
1410	  classDef animate stroke-dasharray: 9,5,stroke-dashoffset: 900,animation: dash 25s linear infinite;
1411	  class e1 animate
1412	```
1413	
1414	In this snippet:
1415	
1416	- `e1@-->` creates an edge with ID `e1`.
1417	- `classDef animate` defines a class named `animate` with styling and animation properties.
1418	- `class e1 animate` applies the `animate` class to the edge `e1`.
1419	
1420	**Note on Escaping Commas:**
1421	When setting the `stroke-dasharray` property, remember to escape commas as `\,` since commas are used as delimiters in Mermaid’s style definitions.

1472	### Minimum length of a link
1473	
1474	Each node in the flowchart is ultimately assigned to a rank in the rendered
1475	graph, i.e. to a vertical or horizontal level (depending on the flowchart
1476	orientation), based on the nodes to which it is linked. By default, links
1477	can span any number of ranks, but you can ask for any link to be longer
1478	than the others by adding extra dashes in the link definition.
1479	
1480	In the following example, two extra dashes are added in the link from node _B_
1481	to node _E_, so that it spans two more ranks than regular links:
1482	
1483	```mermaid-example
1484	flowchart TD
1485	    A[Start] --> B{Is it?}
1486	    B -->|Yes| C[OK]
1487	    C --> D[Rethink]
1488	    D --> B
1489	    B ---->|No| E[End]
1490	```
1491	
1492	```mermaid
1493	flowchart TD
1494	    A[Start] --> B{Is it?}
1495	    B -->|Yes| C[OK]
1496	    C --> D[Rethink]
1497	    D --> B
1498	    B ---->|No| E[End]
1499	```
1500	
1501	> **Note** Links may still be made longer than the requested number of ranks
1502	> by the rendering engine to accommodate other requests.
1503	
1504	When the link label is written in the middle of the link, the extra dashes must
1505	be added on the right side of the link. The following example is equivalent to
1506	the previous one:
1507	
1508	```mermaid-example
1509	flowchart TD
1510	    A[Start] --> B{Is it?}
1511	    B -- Yes --> C[OK]
1512	    C --> D[Rethink]
1513	    D --> B
1514	    B -- No ----> E[End]
1515	```
1516	
1517	```mermaid
1518	flowchart TD
1519	    A[Start] --> B{Is it?}
1520	    B -- Yes --> C[OK]
1521	    C --> D[Rethink]
1522	    D --> B
1523	    B -- No ----> E[End]
1524	```
1525	
1526	For dotted or thick links, the characters to add are equals signs or dots,
1527	as summed up in the following table:
1528	
1529	| Length            |   1    |    2    |    3     |
1530	| ----------------- | :----: | :-----: | :------: |
1531	| Normal            | `---`  | `----`  | `-----`  |
1532	| Normal with arrow | `-->`  | `--->`  | `---->`  |
1533	| Thick             | `===`  | `====`  | `=====`  |
1534	| Thick with arrow  | `==>`  | `===>`  | `====>`  |
1535	| Dotted            | `-.-`  | `-..-`  | `-...-`  |
1536	| Dotted with arrow | `-.->` | `-..->` | `-...->` |

1700	#### Limitation
1701	
1702	If any of a subgraph's nodes are linked to the outside, subgraph direction will be ignored. Instead the subgraph will inherit the direction of the parent graph:
1703	
1704	```mermaid-example
1705	flowchart LR
1706	    subgraph subgraph1
1707	        direction TB
1708	        top1[top] --> bottom1[bottom]
1709	    end
1710	    subgraph subgraph2
1711	        direction TB
1712	        top2[top] --> bottom2[bottom]
1713	    end
1714	    %% ^ These subgraphs are identical, except for the links to them:
1715	
1716	    %% Link *to* subgraph1: subgraph1 direction is maintained
1717	    outside --> subgraph1
1718	    %% Link *within* subgraph2:
1719	    %% subgraph2 inherits the direction of the top-level graph (LR)
1720	    outside ---> top2
1721	```
1722	
1723	```mermaid
1724	flowchart LR
1725	    subgraph subgraph1
1726	        direction TB
1727	        top1[top] --> bottom1[bottom]
1728	    end
1729	    subgraph subgraph2
1730	        direction TB
1731	        top2[top] --> bottom2[bottom]
1732	    end
1733	    %% ^ These subgraphs are identical, except for the links to them:
1734	
1735	    %% Link *to* subgraph1: subgraph1 direction is maintained
1736	    outside --> subgraph1
1737	    %% Link *within* subgraph2:
1738	    %% subgraph2 inherits the direction of the top-level graph (LR)
1739	    outside ---> top2
1740	```
1741	
1742	### Collapsible subgraphs (v11.17.0+)
1743	
1744	A subgraph can be collapsed into a single compact node by attaching the metadata
1745	`@{ view: collapsed }` to its id. This is useful for hiding the internals of a
1746	group while still showing how it connects to the rest of the diagram.
1747	
1748	```mermaid-example
1749	flowchart TD
1750	    Start --> one
1751	    subgraph one [My Group]
1752	        A --> B
1753	        B --> C
1754	    end
1755	    one --> End
1756	    one@{ view: collapsed }
1757	```
1758	
1759	```mermaid
1760	flowchart TD
1761	    Start --> one
1762	    subgraph one [My Group]
1763	        A --> B
1764	        B --> C
1765	    end
1766	    one --> End
1767	    one@{ view: collapsed }
1768	```
1769	
1770	The metadata is attached with the existing `id@{ ... }` statement syntax, where
1771	`id` is the subgraph id (use `subgraph id [Title]` to give a subgraph an explicit
1772	id). When a subgraph is collapsed:
1773	
1774	- Its internal nodes are hidden and it is drawn as a single node carrying the
1775	  subgraph's title.
1776	- Edges that cross the subgraph boundary are **redirected to the collapsed node**.
1777	- Edges that are entirely internal to the collapsed subgraph are dropped (they
1778	  would otherwise become self-loops on the collapsed node).
1779	- For nested subgraphs, a collapse resolves to the **outermost** collapsed
1780	  ancestor, so an edge pointing at a deeply nested node lands on the outermost
1781	  collapsed group.
1782	
1783	`view: expanded` is the default and renders the subgraph normally, so omitting the
1784	metadata (or setting `view: expanded`) keeps the existing behavior.
1785	
1786	## Markdown Strings
1787	
1788	The "Markdown Strings" feature enhances flowcharts and mind maps by offering a more versatile string type, which supports text formatting options such as bold and italics, and automatically wraps text within labels.
1789	
1790	```mermaid-example
1791	---
1792	config:
1793	  htmlLabels: false
1794	---
1795	flowchart LR
1796	subgraph "One"
1797	  a("`The **cat**
1798	  in the hat`") -- "edge label" --> b{{"`The **dog** in the hog`"}}
1799	end
1800	subgraph "`**Two**`"
1801	  c("`The **cat**
1802	  in the hat`") -- "`Bold **edge label**`" --> d("The dog in the hog")
1803	end
1804	```
1805	
1806	```mermaid
1807	---
1808	config:
1809	  htmlLabels: false
1810	---
1811	flowchart LR
1812	subgraph "One"
1813	  a("`The **cat**
1814	  in the hat`") -- "edge label" --> b{{"`The **dog** in the hog`"}}
1815	end
1816	subgraph "`**Two**`"
1817	  c("`The **cat**
1818	  in the hat`") -- "`Bold **edge label**`" --> d("The dog in the hog")
1819	end
1820	```
1821	
1822	Formatting:
1823	
1824	- For bold text, use double asterisks (`**`) before and after the text.
1825	- For italics, use single asterisks (`*`) before and after the text.
1826	- With traditional strings, you needed to add `<br>` tags for text to wrap in nodes. However, markdown strings automatically wrap text when it becomes too long and allows you to start a new line by simply using a newline character instead of a `<br>` tag.
1827	
1828	This feature is applicable to node labels, edge labels, and subgraph labels.
1829	
1830	The auto wrapping can be disabled by using
1831	
1832	```
1833	---
1834	config:
1835	  markdownAutoWrap: false
1836	---
1837	graph LR
1838	```
1839	
1840	## Interaction
1841	
1842	It is possible to bind a click event to a node, the click can lead to either a javascript callback or to a link which will be opened in a new browser tab.
1843	
1844	> **Note**
1845	> This functionality is disabled when using `securityLevel='strict'` and enabled when using `securityLevel='loose'`.
1846	
1847	```
1848	click nodeId callback
1849	click nodeId call callback()
1850	```
1851	
1852	- nodeId is the id of the node
1853	- callback is the name of a javascript function defined on the page displaying the graph, the function will be called with the nodeId as parameter.
1854	
1855	Examples of tooltip usage below:
1856	
1857	```html
1858	<script>
1859	  window.callback = function () {
1860	    alert('A callback was triggered');
1861	  };
1862	</script>
1863	```
1864	
1865	The tooltip text is surrounded in double quotes. The styles of the tooltip are set by the class `.mermaidTooltip`.
1866	
1867	```mermaid-example
1868	flowchart LR
1869	    A-->B
1870	    B-->C
1871	    C-->D
1872	    click A callback "Tooltip for a callback"
1873	    click B "https://www.github.com" "This is a tooltip for a link"
1874	    click C call callback() "Tooltip for a callback"
1875	    click D href "https://www.github.com" "This is a tooltip for a link"
1876	```
1877	
1878	```mermaid
1879	flowchart LR
1880	    A-->B
1881	    B-->C
1882	    C-->D
1883	    click A callback "Tooltip for a callback"
1884	    click B "https://www.github.com" "This is a tooltip for a link"
1885	    click C call callback() "Tooltip for a callback"
1886	    click D href "https://www.github.com" "This is a tooltip for a link"
1887	```
1888	
1889	> **Success** The tooltip functionality and the ability to link to urls are available from version 0.5.2.
1890	
1891	?> Due to limitations with how Docsify handles JavaScript callback functions, an alternate working demo for the above code can be viewed at [this jsfiddle](https://jsfiddle.net/yk4h7qou/2/).
1892	
1893	Links are opened in the same browser tab/window by default. It is possible to change this by adding a link target to the click definition (`_self`, `_blank`, `_parent` and `_top` are supported):
1894	
1895	```mermaid-example
1896	flowchart LR
1897	    A-->B
1898	    B-->C
1899	    C-->D
1900	    D-->E
1901	    click A "https://www.github.com" _blank
1902	    click B "https://www.github.com" "Open this in a new tab" _blank
1903	    click C href "https://www.github.com" _blank
1904	    click D href "https://www.github.com" "Open this in a new tab" _blank
1905	```
1906	
1907	```mermaid
1908	flowchart LR
1909	    A-->B
1910	    B-->C
1911	    C-->D
1912	    D-->E
1913	    click A "https://www.github.com" _blank
1914	    click B "https://www.github.com" "Open this in a new tab" _blank
1915	    click C href "https://www.github.com" _blank
1916	    click D href "https://www.github.com" "Open this in a new tab" _blank
1917	```
1918	
1919	Beginner's tip—a full example using interactive links in a html context:
1920	
1921	```html
1922	<body>
1923	  <pre class="mermaid">
1924	    flowchart LR
1925	        A-->B
1926	        B-->C
1927	        C-->D
1928	        click A callback "Tooltip"
1929	        click B "https://www.github.com" "This is a link"
1930	        click C call callback() "Tooltip"
1931	        click D href "https://www.github.com" "This is a link"
1932	  </pre>
1933	
1934	  <script>
1935	    window.callback = function () {
1936	      alert('A callback was triggered');
1937	    };
1938	    const config = {
1939	      startOnLoad: true,
1940	      htmlLabels: true,
1941	      flowchart: { useMaxWidth: true, curve: 'cardinal' },
1942	      securityLevel: 'loose',
1943	    };
1944	    mermaid.initialize(config);
1945	  </script>
1946	</body>
1947	```
1948	
1949	### Comments
1950	
1951	Comments can be entered within a flow diagram, which will be ignored by the parser. Comments need to be on their own line, and must be prefaced with `%%` (double percent signs). Any text after the start of the comment to the next newline will be treated as a comment, including any flow syntax
1952	
1953	```mermaid-example
1954	flowchart LR
1955	%% this is a comment A -- text --> B{node}
1956	   A -- text --> B -- text2 --> C
1957	```
1958	
1959	```mermaid
1960	flowchart LR
1961	%% this is a comment A -- text --> B{node}
1962	   A -- text --> B -- text2 --> C
1963	```
1964	
1965	## Styling and classes
1966	
1967	### Styling links
1968	
1969	It is possible to style links. For instance, you might want to style a link that is going backwards in the flow. As links
1970	have no ids in the same way as nodes, some other way of deciding what style the links should be attached to is required.
1971	Instead of ids, the order number of when the link was defined in the graph is used, or use default to apply to all links.
1972	In the example below the style defined in the linkStyle statement will belong to the fourth link in the graph:
1973	
1974	```
1975	linkStyle 3 stroke:#ff3,stroke-width:4px,color:red;
1976	```
1977	
1978	It is also possible to add style to multiple links in a single statement, by separating link numbers with commas:
1979	
1980	```
1981	linkStyle 1,2,7 color:blue;
1982	```
1983	
1984	### Styling line curves
1985	
1986	It is possible to style the type of curve used for lines between items, if the default method does not meet your needs.
1987	Available curve styles include `basis`, `bumpX`, `bumpY`, `cardinal`, `catmullRom`, `linear`, `monotoneX`, `monotoneY`,
1988	`natural`, `step`, `stepAfter`, and `stepBefore`.
1989	
1990	For a full list of available curves, including an explanation of custom curves, refer to
1991	the [Shapes](https://d3js.org/d3-shape/curve) documentation in the [d3-shape](https://github.com/d3/d3-shape/) project.
1992	
1993	Line styling can be achieved in two ways:
1994	
1995	1. Change the curve style of all the lines
1996	2. Change the curve style of a particular line
1997	
1998	#### Diagram level curve style
1999	
2000	In this example, a left-to-right graph uses the `stepBefore` curve style:
2001	
2002	```
2003	---
2004	config:
2005	  flowchart:
2006	    curve: stepBefore
2007	---
2008	graph LR
2009	```
2010	
2011	#### Edge level curve style using Edge IDs (v11.10.0+)
2012	
2013	You can assign IDs to [edges](#attaching-an-id-to-edges). After assigning an ID you can modify the line style by modifying the edge's `curve` property using the following syntax:
2014	
2015	```mermaid-example
2016	flowchart LR
2017	    A e1@==> B
2018	    A e2@--> C
2019	    e1@{ curve: linear }
2020	    e2@{ curve: natural }
2021	```
2022	
2023	```mermaid
2024	flowchart LR
2025	    A e1@==> B
2026	    A e2@--> C
2027	    e1@{ curve: linear }
2028	    e2@{ curve: natural }
2029	```
2030	
2031	```info
2032	Any edge curve style modified at the edge level overrides the diagram level style.
2033	```
2034	
2035	```info
2036	If the same edge is modified multiple times the last modification will be rendered.
2037	```
2038	
2039	### Styling a node
2040	
2041	It is possible to apply specific styles such as a thicker border or a different background color to a node.
2042	
2043	```mermaid-example
2044	flowchart LR
2045	    id1(Start)-->id2(Stop)
2046	    style id1 fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px
2047	    style id2 fill:#bbf,stroke:#f66,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,stroke-dasharray: 5 5
2048	```
2049	
2050	```mermaid
2051	flowchart LR
2052	    id1(Start)-->id2(Stop)
2053	    style id1 fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px
2054	    style id2 fill:#bbf,stroke:#f66,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,stroke-dasharray: 5 5
2055	```
2056	
2057	#### Classes
2058	
2059	More convenient than defining the style every time is to define a class of styles and attach this class to the nodes that
2060	should have a different look.
2061	
2062	A class definition looks like the example below:
2063	
2064	```
2065	    classDef className fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px;
2066	```
2067	
2068	Also, it is possible to define style to multiple classes in one statement:
2069	
2070	```
2071	    classDef firstClassName,secondClassName font-size:12pt;
2072	```
2073	
2074	Attachment of a class to a node is done as per below:
2075	
2076	```
2077	    class nodeId1 className;
2078	```
2079	
2080	It is also possible to attach a class to a list of nodes in one statement:
2081	
2082	```
2083	    class nodeId1,nodeId2 className;
2084	```
2085	
2086	A shorter form of adding a class is to attach the classname to the node using the `:::`operator as per below:
2087	
2088	```mermaid-example
2089	flowchart LR
2090	    A:::someclass --> B
2091	    classDef someclass fill:#f96
2092	```
2093	
2094	```mermaid
2095	flowchart LR
2096	    A:::someclass --> B
2097	    classDef someclass fill:#f96
2098	```
2099	
2100	This form can be used when declaring multiple links between nodes:
2101	
2102	```mermaid-example
2103	flowchart LR
2104	    A:::foo & B:::bar --> C:::foobar
2105	    classDef foo stroke:#f00
2106	    classDef bar stroke:#0f0
2107	    classDef foobar stroke:#00f
2108	```
2109	
2110	```mermaid
2111	flowchart LR
2112	    A:::foo & B:::bar --> C:::foobar
2113	    classDef foo stroke:#f00
2114	    classDef bar stroke:#0f0
2115	    classDef foobar stroke:#00f
2116	```
2117	
2118	### CSS classes
2119	
2120	> **Note:** Applying styles to Mermaid nodes via external CSS (e.g., `.cssClass > rect { fill: ... }`) does **not** work reliably. Mermaid's internal styles are injected with `!important` and scoped to the SVG element ID, giving them higher specificity than external CSS rules. External CSS will be silently overridden.
2121	>
2122	> The recommended approach is to use the `classDef` syntax shown in the [Classes](#classes) section above, which works correctly and is the intended styling mechanism.
2123	>
2124	> If external CSS is strictly required, every property must use `!important` to override Mermaid's styles — but this is not recommended.
2125	
2126	**Working approach — use `classDef` instead:**
2127	
2128	```mermaid-example
2129	flowchart LR
2130	    A:::myStyle --> B
2131	    classDef myStyle fill:#ff0000,stroke:#ffff00,stroke-width:4px
2132	```
2133	
2134	```mermaid
2135	flowchart LR
2136	    A:::myStyle --> B
2137	    classDef myStyle fill:#ff0000,stroke:#ffff00,stroke-width:4px
2138	```
2139	
2140	### Default class
2141	
2142	If a class is named default it will be assigned to all classes without specific class definitions.
2143	
2144	```
2145	    classDef default fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px;
2146	```
2147	
2148	## Basic support for fontawesome
2149	
2150	It is possible to add icons from fontawesome.
2151	
2152	The icons are accessed via the syntax fa:#icon class name#.
2153	
2154	```mermaid-example
2155	flowchart TD
2156	    B["fa:fa-twitter for peace"]
2157	    B-->C[fa:fa-ban forbidden]
2158	    B-->D(fa:fa-spinner)
2159	    B-->E(A fa:fa-camera-retro perhaps?)
2160	```
2161	
2162	```mermaid
2163	flowchart TD
2164	    B["fa:fa-twitter for peace"]
2165	    B-->C[fa:fa-ban forbidden]
2166	    B-->D(fa:fa-spinner)
2167	    B-->E(A fa:fa-camera-retro perhaps?)
2168	```
2169	
2170	There are two ways to display these FontAwesome icons:
2171	
2172	### Register FontAwesome icon packs (v11.7.0+)
2173	
2174	You can register your own FontAwesome icon pack following the ["Registering icon packs" instructions](../config/icons.md).
2175	
2176	Supported prefixes: `fa`, `fab`, `fas`, `far`, `fal`, `fad`.
2177	
2178	> **Note**
2179	> Note that it will fall back to FontAwesome CSS if FontAwesome packs are not registered.
2180	
2181	### Register FontAwesome CSS
2182	
2183	Mermaid supports Font Awesome if the CSS is included on the website.
2184	Mermaid does not have any restriction on the version of Font Awesome that can be used.
2185	
2186	Please refer the [Official Font Awesome Documentation](https://fontawesome.com/start) on how to include it in your website.
2187	
2188	Adding this snippet in the `<head>` would add support for Font Awesome v6.5.1
2189	
2190	```html
2191	<link
2192	  href="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/font-awesome/6.5.1/css/all.min.css"
2193	  rel="stylesheet"
2194	/>
2195	```
2196	
2197	### Custom icons
2198	
2199	It is possible to use custom icons served from Font Awesome as long as the website imports the corresponding kit.
2200	
2201	Note that this is currently a paid feature from Font Awesome.
2202	
2203	For custom icons, you need to use the `fak` prefix.
2204	
2205	**Example**
2206	
2207	```
2208	flowchart TD
2209	    B[fa:fa-twitter] %% standard icon
2210	    B-->E(fak:fa-custom-icon-name) %% custom icon
2211	```
2212	
2213	And trying to render it
2214	
2215	```mermaid-example
2216	flowchart TD
2217	    B["fa:fa-twitter for peace"]
2218	    B-->C["fab:fa-truck-bold a custom icon"]
2219	```
2220	
2221	```mermaid
2222	flowchart TD
2223	    B["fa:fa-twitter for peace"]
2224	    B-->C["fab:fa-truck-bold a custom icon"]
2225	```
2226	
2227	## Graph declarations with spaces between vertices and link and without semicolon
2228	
2229	- In graph declarations, the statements also can now end without a semicolon. After release 0.2.16, ending a graph statement with semicolon is just optional. So the below graph declaration is also valid along with the old declarations of the graph.
2230	
2231	- A single space is allowed between vertices and the link. However there should not be any space between a vertex and its text and a link and its text. The old syntax of graph declaration will also work and hence this new feature is optional and is introduced to improve readability.
2232	
2233	Below is the new declaration of the graph edges which is also valid along with the old declaration of the graph edges.
2234	
2235	```mermaid-example
2236	flowchart LR
2237	    A[Hard edge] -->|Link text| B(Round edge)
2238	    B --> C{Decision}
2239	    C -->|One| D[Result one]
2240	    C -->|Two| E[Result two]
2241	```
2242	
2243	```mermaid
2244	flowchart LR
2245	    A[Hard edge] -->|Link text| B(Round edge)
2246	    B --> C{Decision}
2247	    C -->|One| D[Result one]
2248	    C -->|Two| E[Result two]
2249	```
2250	
2251	## Configuration
2252	
2253	### Renderer
2254	
2255	The layout of the diagram is done with the layout algorithm. The default is
2256	[ELK](https://www.eclipse.org/elk/), which handles larger and more complex
2257	diagrams well and is bundled with Mermaid.
2258	
2259	To use the classic Dagre layout instead:
2260	
2261	```
2262	config:
2263	  layout: dagre
2264	```
2265	
2266	The `flowchart-elk` diagram type still works, but is no longer needed — it
2267	predates `layout` and selected what is now the default.
2268	
2269	The `defaultRenderer` option of the `flowchart`, `class` and `state` config
2270	sections was removed in v12. It named a rendering engine at a time when there
2271	was more than one; all of its values had come to mean the same renderer, and
2272	its `elk` value only ever set `layout: elk` on your behalf. Use `layout`
2273	directly.
2274	
2275	### Width
2276	
2277	It is possible to adjust the width of the rendered flowchart.
2278	
2279	This is done by defining **mermaid.flowchartConfig** or by the CLI to use a JSON file with the configuration. How to use the CLI is described in the mermaidCLI page.
2280	mermaid.flowchartConfig can be set to a JSON string with config parameters or the corresponding object.
2281	
2282	```javascript
2283	mermaid.flowchartConfig = {
2284	    width: 100%
2285	}
2286	```

# Flowcharts - Basic Syntax

Flowcharts are composed of **nodes** (geometric shapes) and **edges** (arrows or lines). The Mermaid code defines how nodes and edges are made and accommodates different arrow types, multi-directional arrows, and any linking to and from subgraphs.

> **Warning**
> If you are using the word "end" in a Flowchart node, capitalize the entire word or any of the letters (e.g., "End" or "END"), or apply this [workaround](https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/issues/1444#issuecomment-639528897). Typing "end" in all lowercase letters will break the Flowchart.

> **Warning**
> If you are using the letter "o" or "x" as the first letter in a connecting Flowchart node, add a space before the letter or capitalize the letter (e.g., "dev--- ops", "dev---Ops").
>
> Typing "A---oB" will create a [circle edge](#circle-edge-example).
>
> Typing "A---xB" will create a [cross edge](#cross-edge-example).

### A node (default)

```mermaid-example
---
title: Node
---
flowchart LR
    id
```

```mermaid
---
title: Node
---
flowchart LR
    id
```

> **Note**
> The id is what is displayed in the box.

> **💡 Tip**
> Instead of `flowchart` one can also use `graph`.

### A node with text

It is also possible to set text in the box that differs from the id. If this is done several times, it is the last text
found for the node that will be used. Also if you define edges for the node later on, you can omit text definitions. The
one previously defined will be used when rendering the box.

```mermaid-example
---
title: Node with text
---
flowchart LR
    id1[This is the text in the box]
```

```mermaid
---
title: Node with text
---
flowchart LR
    id1[This is the text in the box]
```

#### Unicode text

Use `"` to enclose the unicode text.

```mermaid-example
flowchart LR
    id["This ❤ Unicode"]
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    id["This ❤ Unicode"]
```

#### Markdown formatting

Use double quotes and backticks "\` text \`" to enclose the markdown text.

```mermaid-example
---
config:
  htmlLabels: false
---
flowchart LR
    markdown["`This **is** _Markdown_`"]
    newLines["`Line1
    Line 2
    Line 3`"]
    markdown --> newLines
```

```mermaid
---
config:
  htmlLabels: false
---
flowchart LR
    markdown["`This **is** _Markdown_`"]
    newLines["`Line1
    Line 2
    Line 3`"]
    markdown --> newLines
```

### Direction

This statement declares the direction of the Flowchart.

This declares the flowchart is oriented from top to bottom (`TD` or `TB`).

```mermaid-example
flowchart TD
    Start --> Stop
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start --> Stop
```

This declares the flowchart is oriented from left to right (`LR`).

```mermaid-example
flowchart LR
    Start --> Stop
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Start --> Stop
```

Possible FlowChart orientations are:

- TB - Top to bottom
- TD - Top-down/ same as top to bottom
- BT - Bottom to top
- RL - Right to left
- LR - Left to right

## Default theme, look and layout (v12.0.0+)

Flowcharts use the `redux-color` theme and the `neo` look by default, and are laid out by [ELK](https://www.eclipse.org/elk/) rather than Dagre. Not every diagram type
does — see [Per-diagram defaults](../config/theming.md#per-diagram-defaults) for the list and
for the order in which Mermaid decides.

The same diagram, drawn both ways:

### With the defaults

```mermaid-example
flowchart LR
  subgraph Client
    UI[Web app]
    Cache[(Local cache)]
  end
  subgraph Services
    API[API gateway]
    Auth[Auth service]
    Orders[Order service]
```

## Expanded Node Shapes in Mermaid Flowcharts (v11.3.0+)

Mermaid introduces 30 new shapes to enhance the flexibility and precision of flowchart creation. These new shapes provide more options to represent processes, decisions, events, data storage visually, and other elements within your flowcharts, improving clarity and semantic meaning.

New Syntax for Shape Definition

Mermaid now supports a general syntax for defining shape types to accommodate the growing number of shapes. This syntax allows you to assign specific shapes to nodes using a clear and flexible format:

```
A@{ shape: rect }
```

This syntax creates a node A as a rectangle. It renders in the same way as `A["A"]`, or `A`.
